author: skill agent (ADR-22)
note: The five-prompt trigger test prompts/skill-agent.md requires, plus one confusion case per neighbouring skill in the library. Run with skills/_validation/trigger_test.py. Revised 2026-11-02 (ADR-38 length retrofit, 362 lines to 109): rhsi-pos-3 is retired with section 8 (see retired_cases) rather than rewritten, because the skill no longer answers the question and a pass would be the wrong outcome. Two positives replace it, one for each live delta that had no positive case of its own, delta 3 (attribution as search) and delta 5 (feedback cost), which is the gap retiring one case made visible rather than created. rhsi-conf-1 was rewritten earlier the same day for a different reason, recorded on the case.

cases.prompt: We built a nightly job where the agent reads its own failed runs, writes a patch to its own prompts and tool code, and applies it. Four rounds in, the score on the task set it evolves against keeps climbing and real customer tickets are no better. What is going wrong?
cases.anchor: when self-edits raise the benchmark score but real tasks do not improve
cases.rationale: This is section 6 exactly, the contaminated evolution set, and section 5's missing diff-review gate behind it. Two activation clauses match and the failure named is the one the skill's evidence explains.

cases.prompt: Our agent rewrites parts of its own scaffold between runs. What should decide whether a proposed edit is kept or rolled back, and how much should one edit be allowed to change at once?
cases.anchor: when choosing the gate that accepts or rolls back a proposed edit
cases.rationale: Sections 4 and 5 are the whole answer, and the wrong default (accept if the diagnosis that motivated the edit looks sound) is what a builder reaches for unaided.

cases.prompt: Our agent's run logs are hundreds of thousands of tokens long, and when a run fails we cannot tell which function in the scaffold caused it. Right now a judge model reads the log once and names a culprit. Should we pay for a stronger judge?
cases.anchor: when attributing a failure to one function inside a long execution log
cases.rationale: Written 2026-11-02 to replace rhsi-pos-3. Delta 3 is the best-evidenced delta in the file and had no positive case before this, and it is the delta three confusion cases in other skills' files now point at, so the suite was asserting coverage it never tested from the inside. The decision the prompt is about to get wrong is the one delta 3 answers with a number: buy search turns before a bigger diagnostician, because a lower-tier judge with four turns of continual search matched a higher-tier judge with one pass. Phrased in the vocabulary a requester would use rather than the library's, which is the he-pos-1 lesson from the same run.

cases.prompt: Our self-editing loop only gets through two candidate edits a night, because every candidate has to be run against the live environment before we know whether to keep it, so it never does enough cycles to converge. Is there a way to score a candidate before it touches a real run?
cases.anchor: when the loop's own feedback costs more than its edits gain
cases.rationale: Written 2026-11-02 to replace rhsi-pos-3. Delta 5 had no positive case. The prompt names the delta's own decision, which is the cost of evaluating a candidate, and the answer is Dream-RSI's replay tree: score candidate policies inside a simulator built from the discovery history and deploy only the survivor. First draft of this case asked instead whether to compact the context at a fixed seventy percent of the window, and it routed to context-window-engineering at the first run. That was the case's defect and not the library's: compaction is one of three mechanisms delta 5 lifts and it is a mechanism the neighbour owns outright, so a positive case built on it tests a boundary rather than this delta. Re-aimed at the half no other skill covers. The compaction arithmetic is still tested, by eval task rhsi-t8, where it belongs, because it is checkable as a number rather than as a routing decision.

cases.prompt: Our release pipeline should automatically roll back a deploy when the error rate climbs after a push. What thresholds and bake time should we set, and who gets paged when it trips?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: roll back, automatic, gate, threshold, measure and improve are all this skill's own vocabulary, and the sentence is about a system changing itself without a human. But the artifact is a release, nothing is diagnosing or rewriting a scaffold, and the real need is incident practice. A description matching on rollback alone would fire here.

cases.prompt: Our nightly job regenerates the API client from the vendor's OpenAPI spec, and the diffs it produces keep failing code review. How should we structure the regeneration and the review step so this stops?
cases.rationale: Hard negative: an automated process that writes code, produces diffs, and has a review gate that rejects them, which is the shape of section 5. But the generator is a deterministic codegen tool with no diagnosis loop and nothing it learns from the rejection, so none of this skill's evidence applies. The nearest honest match is ordinary integration work.

cases.prompt: We are going to evolve our agent's harness rather than train the model, and our own engineers will write each change by hand this sprint. Is harness work really the better spend than fine-tuning, and in what order?
cases.rationale: Belongs to the neighbour. It borrows this skill's headline vocabulary (evolve the harness, not the weights) but a person writes every change, so the answer is harness-engineering's harness-before-weights ordering and its negative expected sign on the imitation fine-tune, not this skill's gates and freeze lists. Routing it here would hand the reader machinery for an automation that does not exist. Rewritten 2026-11-02: the prompt also asked how to tell which sub-agent is at fault. That clause was testing two things this case cannot test. The 2026-09-30 ADR-38 rewrite of harness-engineering cut the localisation half of its debugging section, on a bare-arm screen that found the subject supplied it unprompted, and that file's own provenance names the cut. So expecting harness-engineering to win a sub-agent-attribution prompt has been a false claim about a skill behaving correctly since that day, and it was reported as this suite's failure for 32 days. And failure localisation is now this skill's own section 3, so the clause argued for the owning skill inside a case whose whole point is that the owning skill loses. Both halves of the defect are the clause's, so the clause is gone and the live harness-versus-weights question is what the case now asks.

cases.prompt: We want the agent's own successful rollouts to become the training data for the next fine-tune of the model itself. How do we decide which rollouts are good enough to train on, and how do we keep the run from collapsing?
cases.rationale: Belongs to the other neighbour. Self-referential improvement again, and the words loop, own rollouts and improve itself all appear, but the thing being updated is the weights, which is the boundary this skill's description draws explicitly. Routing it here would give scaffold-edit gates to a question about teacher gating and collapse.

retired_cases.prompt: Thirteen coding agents are committing to one shared repository trying to push the same metric, and for five days every one of them has been building on the same idea. How do we get the exploration spread out again?
retired_cases.anchor: when several agents rewrite one shared codebase and converge on the same idea
retired_cases.rationale: The Agora monoculture finding is the only evidence in the library that speaks to a population of self-editing agents collapsing, and the diversity-signal answer is not obvious.
retired_cases.retired: 2026-11-02. This case tested the trigger 'when several agents rewrite one shared codebase and converge on the same idea', and the ADR-38 length retrofit cut section 8, the Agora population finding, along with that clause of the description. It is retired rather than rewritten because the skill no longer answers the question, so a pass would be the wrong outcome, which is the handling ac-pos-3 received on 2026-10-06. It passed on its last run before retirement and went to silence the moment the description clause left, which is the engine agreeing that the clause was the whole of its coverage. The finding is queued in docs/research/reading-queue.md for a seat that can give it a page, and nothing in this library covers it today.
